newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-World market drives Australia sorghum - Grainco.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-World market drives Australia sorghum - Grainco.

text.p: Australian sorghum prices continued to be predominantly driven by international factors, Rob Brealey, trading manager of Queensland cooperative Grainco Ltd, said in the weekly market review.
Both southern and central Queensland growing areas were producing exportable surpluses but southern surpluses were less than that expected for central Queensland.
However, attempts by southern Queensland prices to move higher over the past fortnight had not been supported by genuine domestic consumer buying interest, he said.

With patchy but heavy rainfall having occurred across some areas of south Queensland over the weekend, and more rain forecast for this week, any higher price moves could be limited in the short-term, he said.
Internationally, feed grain buying interest in Asia remained very subdued.
Aggressive selling by Argentina and China in Asia would continue to place pressure on other origins, including Australia, he said.
The international feed barley market was relatively quiet, apart from price adjustments in Europe, suggesting a slightly lower outlook in the Australian price, he said.
This, together with scattered rain throughout southern Queensland, should prompt a quiet trade again this week, with values following the underlying sorghum price, he said.
The international malting barley market was very quiet with most first quarter demand satisfied from Australian production.
Deferred values were coming under pressure as Australian production of about 2.5 million tonnes appeared sufficient to cover export demand in the medium-term, he said.
Domestically, values were steady over the past week, with Grainco's malting barley cash bid finishing the week at A$184.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane.
Export interest in cottonseed was beginning to re-surface after a very quiet Christmas and New Year period, he said.
There was evidence that the Japanese market was still to complete coverage of cottonseed for the balance of old crop months of February and March.
With the new crop delayed slightly because of mild conditions, consumers may not be able to extend coverage too much further without making additional purchases, he said.
Old crop demand could possibly total 10,000 tonnes, ensuring there would be very little old crop carry-out, he said.
The domestic market remains subdued with some parcels of new crop business at around the A$110-A$115 a tonne ex gin level, he said.
With crop prospects continuing to indicate a record 1997 Australian cotton crop, the majority of domestic consumers were holding off making substantial new crop commitments, he said.
